learn.b: An object stores related data as key-value pairs inside curly braces. Each key is a name and each value can be anything: a number, a string, an array or even another object. Pairs are separated by commas.

Use dot notation, person.name, when you know the key. Use bracket notation, person["name"], when the key is in a variable or has spaces. Assigning to a key changes it, or adds it if it does not exist. Reading a missing key gives undefined.
The delete keyword removes a key. The in operator checks whether a key exists. Nested objects are read by chaining dots, like person.address.city.
Object.keys gives an array of the keys, Object.values gives the values and Object.entries gives [key, value] pairs. Use for...in to loop over the keys of an object.

qs.q: How do you read the name property of person?
qs.why: Dot notation reads a property.

qs.why: delete obj.key removes the key.

learn.b: A method is a function stored in an object property. Call it with dot notation and brackets. The short form lets you leave out the colon and the function keyword.
Inside a method, this refers to the object the method was called on. That lets a method read and change the object own data. Without this, the method would not know which object it belongs to.

An arrow function does not have its own this. If you use an arrow as an object method, this will not be the object. So for methods, use the normal method syntax. Arrows are great inside methods, where they keep the outer this.
If a method ends with return this, you can chain calls like obj.add(1).add(2). Be careful: pulling a method out of its object, like let f = obj.method, loses this, so f() will not work as expected.

qs.q: Inside a method, what does this refer to?
o: The object the method is called on
qs.why: this is the object before the dot.

qs.q: Which is the method shorthand?
qs.why: Shorthand drops the colon and function keyword.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: The first call returns 1 and the second returns 2, so 1 + 2 = 3.

qs.q: An arrow function used as an object method has this set to that object.
qs.why: Arrow functions have no own this.

learn.b: Destructuring pulls values out of an object into variables in one line. The names inside the braces must match the keys. You can rename with a colon and give a default with =.
Array destructuring uses square brackets and picks items by position. You can skip an item by leaving a gap. It also gives a neat swap without a temporary variable.

Three dots spread an array or object into its pieces. Use it to copy or combine them without changing the originals. For objects, later keys win over earlier ones. The copy is shallow, so nested objects are still shared.
In a function definition, three dots collect all remaining arguments into an array. This lets a function accept any number of values. In destructuring, rest collects whatever is left over.

qs.q: What is a after const { a } = { a: 1, b: 2 }?
qs.why: The key a has the value 1.

qs.q: { ...o } creates a new object that has the properties of o.
qs.why: Spread copies the properties into a new object.

learn.b: map runs a function on every item and returns a new array of the results, always the same length as the original. The original array is not changed.
filter runs a test function on each item and returns a new array with only the items for which the test gave a truthy value. The result can be shorter, or even empty.

reduce boils an array down to one value. Your function gets an accumulator (the running result) and the current item, and returns the new accumulator. The second argument of reduce is the starting value. The result can be a number, string, array or object.
Because map and filter return arrays, you can chain calls one after another. Read a chain from left to right: filter first, then map, then reduce. This replaces many small loops with clear steps.
learn.code:
let total = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  .filter(n => n % 2 === 1)
  .map(n => n * 10)
  .reduce((a, n) => a + n, 0);
console.log(total); // 90

qs.q: What does map return?
o: A new array of the same length
qs.why: map transforms each item into a new array.

qs.q: filter keeps the items for which the callback returns...
qs.why: Truthy results keep the item.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: filter keeps 2 and 4, then map multiplies by 10.

qs.q: reduce can only be used to add numbers.
qs.why: reduce can build any kind of single result.

learn.b: find returns the first item that passes your test, or undefined if none does. findIndex returns its position, or -1. Both stop as soon as they find a match.
some returns true if at least one item passes the test. every returns true only if all items pass. On an empty array, some gives false and every gives true.

sort puts items in order, but it changes the original array. By default it compares items as text, so numbers sort in a surprising order. Give it a compare function: (a, b) => a - b sorts numbers upward and (a, b) => b - a sorts downward.

To keep the original order, sort a copy made with the spread syntax. reverse flips an array in place. For strings, the default sort works alphabetically, and localeCompare is the proper compare function for words.

qs.q: What does find return when no item passes?
qs.why: find gives undefined when nothing matches.

qs.q: What does some return?
o: true if at least one item passes
qs.why: some means at least one.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: Default sort compares as text, so 10 comes before 9.

qs.q: sort() with no argument sorts numbers from smallest to largest.
qs.why: It sorts as text, so 10 comes before 9.

qs.why: All three items are above 0.

qs.q: Arrange the lines to sort ages numerically and print them
qs.why: Sort before printing.

A positive result puts b first

learn.b: split cuts a string into an array at a separator, and join glues an array back into a string. Splitting on an empty string "" gives single characters. reverse flips an array, so split, reverse, join reverses text.
learn.code:
console.log("a-b-c".split("-").length); // 3
console.log("abc".split("").reverse().join("")); // cba

learn.b: trim removes spaces and new lines from both ends. trimStart and trimEnd do one side. These are very useful for cleaning up what users type. Remember strings are immutable, so each method returns a new string.
learn.code:
let s = "  hi  ";
console.log(s.trim().toUpperCase()); // HI

learn.b: includes tells if some text is inside. startsWith and endsWith check the ends. indexOf returns the position of the first match or -1. slice(start, end) cuts out a piece, and a negative start counts from the end.
learn.code:
let s = "Hello World";
console.log(s.includes("World")); // true
console.log(s.startsWith("He")); // true
console.log(s.slice(0, 5)); // Hello
console.log(s.slice(-5)); // World

learn.b: replace swaps the first match, while replaceAll swaps every match. repeat copies a string several times. padStart adds characters to the front until a length is reached, which is handy for times like 07.
learn.code:
console.log("banana".replaceAll("a", "o")); // bonono
console.log("ab".repeat(3)); // ababab
console.log(String(7).padStart(2, "0")); // 07

qs.why: It strips whitespace at the start and end.

learn.b: Scope decides where a variable can be seen. Variables outside every function are global. let and const are block scoped: they exist only inside the nearest pair of curly braces. The old var keyword is function scoped, which is why it is avoided.

When JavaScript needs a variable it looks in the current scope first, then in the surrounding scopes, going outwards. An inner variable with the same name hides the outer one, which is called shadowing. Inner code can read outer variables but not the other way round.

A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the place where it was created, even after that place has finished running. Returning an inner function from an outer function gives you a function with private memory.

Each call of the outer function makes a fresh set of variables, so every closure has its own private state. Nobody outside can change c directly. Closures power counters, private data and callbacks that remember things.

qs.q: A variable declared with let inside curly braces is visible...
qs.why: let is block scoped.

qs.q: What is a closure?
o: A function that remembers the variables where it was created
A way to close a file
qs.why: A closure keeps access to its outer variables.

qs.why: The same c is shared across calls, so the second call returns 2.

qs.q: Each call to makeCounter creates its own separate count.
qs.why: Every call has fresh variables.

qs.why: The inner x is a different variable.

qs.why: The returned arrow remembers n.

learn.b: A class is a blueprint for making many similar objects. You write class Name, and inside it a constructor and methods. By convention class names start with a capital letter.
Use the new keyword to create an object from a class. The constructor runs automatically and sets up the new object using this. Each object made this way is called an instance and has its own data.

The constructor sets the starting fields. Methods are written without the function keyword and are shared by all instances. A method can change this to update the instance, and it can return this to allow chaining.

A static method belongs to the class itself, not to instances, so you call it as ClassName.method(). A getter, written with the get keyword, is read like a property but runs code. Classes must be called with new, or JavaScript throws an error.

qs.why: new calls the constructor and builds the object.

learn.b: A class can inherit from another class with extends. The new class, called the subclass, gets all the methods of the parent class and can add its own. This avoids copying code.

If the subclass defines a method with the same name, it overrides the parent version. Instances of the subclass use the new one. Inside it, super.method() calls the parent version, so you can extend behaviour instead of replacing it.

If a subclass has its own constructor, it must call super(...) before touching this. super(...) runs the parent constructor, which sets up the inherited fields. After that the subclass can add its own fields.
The instanceof operator tests whether an object was made by a class or one of its parents. A Dog is an instance of Dog and of Animal. This is the is-a relationship: a dog is an animal.

qs.q: Which keyword makes one class inherit from another?
qs.why: class B extends A makes B a subclass of A.

qs.q: What does super(...) do in a subclass constructor?
qs.why: It runs the parent constructor.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: super.hi() gives A, then B is added.

qs.q: In a subclass constructor you must call super before using this.
qs.why: Otherwise JavaScript throws a ReferenceError.

qs.why: A B is also an A.

learn.b: When JavaScript hits an error it stops and prints a message, unless you handle it. Common ones are ReferenceError (a name that does not exist), TypeError (using a value the wrong way, like null.x) and SyntaxError (broken code).
learn.code:
// console.log(nope);  // ReferenceError
// null.x;  // TypeError

learn.b: Put risky code in a try block. If any line inside throws, JavaScript jumps straight to the catch block and the rest of the try is skipped. The catch gets the error object, whose message property describes the problem.
A finally block runs after try and catch no matter what, even if there was no error. It is used for cleanup like closing things. If no error happens, catch is simply skipped.

You can raise an error yourself with throw new Error(message). This stops the function and sends the error to the nearest catch. Use it when someone gives your function bad input. Always throw Error objects, not plain strings.

qs.q: Which block runs when an error is thrown inside try?
qs.why: Control jumps to catch.

qs.q: When does a finally block run?
qs.why: finally always runs.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: null.x throws, so b is skipped and catch runs.

qs.q: throw new Error("x") stops the function unless something catches it.
qs.why: An uncaught error ends the program.

qs.q: Match each keyword to its job
What does try { throw new Error('boom'); } catch (e) { console.log(e.message); } print?
qs.why: e.message holds the text given to Error.

qs.q: Arrange the lines to throw and catch an error
qs.why: The throw is inside the try block.

learn.b: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for sending and storing data. It looks like a JavaScript object but is stricter: keys and strings need double quotes, and it cannot hold functions or undefined. Nearly every web service speaks JSON.
learn.code: {"name":"Ana","age":9,"tags":["a","b"],"ok":true}

learn.b: JSON.stringify turns a JavaScript value into a JSON string. Use it to save or send data. Functions and undefined values inside an object are left out.
JSON.parse turns a JSON string back into a real value. If the text is not valid JSON it throws a SyntaxError, so wrap risky input in try/catch. A stringify then parse round trip makes a deep copy.

Pass a third argument to stringify to indent the output and make it readable, like JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2). The data is the same, only the spacing changes. The second argument is rarely needed, so it is usually null.

qs.q: What does JSON.stringify do?
o: Turns a value into a JSON string
qs.why: stringify makes text from data.

qs.q: What does JSON.parse do?
o: Turns a JSON string into a value
qs.why: parse makes data from text.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: JSON uses double quotes around keys.

qs.q: In JSON, keys must be written inside double quotes.
qs.why: Single quotes or no quotes are invalid JSON.

What does JSON.parse('{"n":5}').n return?
qs.why: The parsed object has n equal to 5.

qs.q: Arrange the lines to save an object as text and read it back
qs.why: Stringify before parse.

learn.b: As programs grow, putting everything in one file gets messy. A module is a file that keeps its own variables private and shares only what it chooses. Modules make code easier to find, reuse and test.
learn.code:
// math.js and app.js are two
// separate files (modules)

learn.b: Use export in front of a function, class or variable to share it. In another file, use import with the names in braces and the file path. Imports go at the top of the file. These are called named exports and must be imported with the same names.
A file can also have one default export, written export default. It is imported without braces, and the importer can choose any name for it. A file can mix one default export with many named ones.

Older code used the module pattern: a function that runs at once, keeps variables private inside and returns an object of public tools. You can still use this idea anywhere. Node.js also has an older style called CommonJS that uses require, but modern code prefers import and export.

qs.q: Which keyword makes something available to other files?
qs.why: export marks code as shareable.

qs.q: What does import { add } from "./math.js" do?
o: Gets the named export add from math.js
qs.why: The braces pick a named export.

qs.q: What does app.js print?
qs.why: add(2, 3) returns 5.

qs.q: A default export can be imported under any name you choose.
qs.why: Only named exports must keep their exact names.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Type the keyword that brings code in from another file.
qs.why: import loads exports from a module.
